comments.author: lucasluitjes

> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. And the "Limitations" section:

Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.
But a long tail of unpatche

comments.author: ievans
comments.text:
Super impressive work by Calif as usual.
The exploit conditions are very specific but there are still going to be a lot of hosts impacted. We at Semgrep published some free detection scripts here:
https://github.com/semgrep/detection-scripts/tree/main/CVE-2...
They look for these five conditions:
* HotSpot VM: any OpenJDK build, Oracle JDK, or GraalVM JDK. Only HotSpot generates the stub. OpenJ9 and GCJ are OK. Azul Prime (Zing), which replaces C2 with its own JIT, and any VM name not recognized as HotSpot are [?], never [!].
* x86-64 JVM on an x86-64 host.
* Version 17.0.6 or later, not at or above a version listed in FIXED_IN, and no newer than the newest releases checked (see below). Newer versions are [?]: they may carry the fix.
* The JVM reports avx512_vbmi and avx512bw, and UseAVX >= 3.
* Base64 intrinsics are on and C2/JVMCI can compile. These turn it off: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, -Xint, -XX:TieredStopAtLevel below 4.

We should probably be measuring deployable merges to main.  The math just doesn't work for pipeline based CI as you add more agents.
Three things matter.
1 -- How many non-conflicting changes can actually be made at one time (Fan Out)
2 -- How long a critical path takes
3 -- How many times you have to run that critical path.  Most orgs run it 2-3x, once before the PR in the agent loop, once in CI, and another in the MQ
This is why most orgs cant get past about 12 PRs an hour.

stories.title_en: Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
Nice. I didn't realize that the US had lost its position in high-end machine tools, too.
Volume in the machine tool business is dependent on the derivative of product production. If product production is trending downward, machine tool sales drop to near zero. They're long-lasting machines, usually good for many decades. There's a sizable used market. The new replacement market is thus small. Machine tools become obsolete, but often, the big iron gets a new controller and goes on cutting metal.
Conversely, if product production is growing, as in China until recently, there's a huge demand for new machine tools.
All those US medium-sized machine tool makers that made gear hobbing machines and such seem to be gone. Along with most of the people who were really into precision machining.
You can't do this stuff with Amazon warehouse level employees.
Robotic joints are an interesting case. They need a small 3-phase motor, which is a lot like a drone motor. They usually have a harmonic drive. And of course they have sensors and a controller. For a long time, robotic joints for mobile robots were put together mostly by grad students in tiny quantities using off the shelf components intend

comments.author: robot_jesus
comments.text:
My kids (16 and 13) both attend schools that recently implemented phone bans and they love it, somewhat surprisingly. They've commented on how one of their favorite things about school is actually the social aspect. Before the ban, at lunch or study halls or recess, kids would just be on their phones and now they're laughing and goofing off, as kids should be doing.
Bonkers to me that we ever allowed this.
Oh, and for context, the kids are allowed to go to the office and check in on a message or send a text (e.g., soccer practice is canceled due to rain, can you pick me up at 4?) during any non-class period so it's still easy to communicate.

comments.text: If it actually ends up improving scores that's a big bonus but there are many other positive things that can come from this like protecting mental health, vision health and more face to face socialization. China banned phones in primary and secondary schools back in 2021.

comments.author: tfirst
comments.text:
The identification in this study is a sketchy, and a similar study in the exact same setting ((
https://tom-dee.github.io/files/w35132.pdf
) doesn't find a significant effect.
1. they see diverging pre-trends, which immediately suggests a problem in the diff-in-diff
2. they're doing some kind of propensity score matching to build a comparison set, and it looks like they're matching across state lines, which is going to expose them to all sorts of weird state-level shocks
3. while the previous study just looked at the impacts on grades, they've built a value-added model and they're estimating their effects through that. That just adds another place where they can get the model wrong and end up with bad estimates.
They also point out that the schools that bought these pouches had more ESSER money, which they could have spent on tutoring.
